newsitem.title: USA: Experts urge limits to genetic tests in workplace.
newsitem.headline: Experts urge limits to genetic tests in workplace.

text.p: Employers should not be able to use genetic tests to discriminate on the job, deny health insurance or violate employee privacy, several top geneticists, ethicists and health advocates said Thursday.

The group made recommendations at a news conference that would restrict an employer's access to information about a worker's genetics and protect the worker from job discrimination. The recommendations, outlined in an essay appearing Friday in the journal Science, say these laws or regulations should be uniform across the country rather than having different levels of protection from one state to another.
At least two bills on genetic privacy issues have been introduced in Congress this year, although no action has been taken yet.

"The use of genetic information in the workplace poses societal risks that have an impact on employment possibilities, health insurance and privacy," the group, which includes Francis Collins, director of the National Human Genome Research Institute at the National Institutes of Health, wrote in Science.

"Individuals who might otherwise believe that they can benefit from genetic testing may decline it because of their fear of employment discrimination and lack of privacy in the workplace," the health lawyers, geneticists and activists said.

Several tests have become available, either in clinical research settings or in the medical community at large, that tell if a person has a gene that predisposes toward a certain disease such as breast or colon cancer. There is already anecdotal evidence that some employers are using this information to squeeze out those employees and their potentially big medical bills, or to limit their health insurance.

Some have conducted gene tests such as for sickle cell anaemia that afflicts black Americans without the workers' informed consent, said Karen Rothenberg, lead author of the Science article and a health law expert at the University of Maryland.

Gene tests tell of a predisposition to a disease. In most cases they cannot tell whether a person is 100 percent certain to get the disease, how severe the disease will be or whether the person would become sick at age 30 or 90. Morever, everyone has some disposition to genetic disease, but not all those genetic flaws have yet been identified in the lab.
"There are no perfect specimens," Collins said, adding that most people probably have 5 to 30 "significant" genetic flaws.

Christina DeMark, a saleswoman from Milwaukee, told the news conference she was fired a month after telling an employer that she had the gene for Huntington's disease, which killed her mother. She said she has no symptoms of the disease.

"They did everything they could to get me to quit ... a month later, they let me go," said DeMark, who found another job and then decided to start her own business. Her employer said she was dismissed for cause unrelated to her medical condition, she said.

The Kassebaum-Kennedy health insurance reform law, enacted last year, gives some protection to people with group health insurance, saying they cannot be excluded from coverage because of a genetic defect. But the law does not take into account the uninsured or people with individual policies and it does not address workplace discrimination issues.
Some states have also begun to pass some genetic privacy legislation, but it varies greatly, Rothenberg said.
